10-year research plan, 2026 to 2035

Cybersecurity in Organizations: Employees' Protective and Risky Security Behaviors

Noah 10-Year Plan: A Research Program in Behavioral Information Security

Huan (Noah) Nguyen
PhD Student, Business Information Technology, Pamplin College of Business, Virginia Tech

The plan in one sentence

Security controls work only when employees choose the protective action.

Employees often bend or go around security controls to get their work done, especially when the work is urgent or the approved system fails. My 10-year plan studies these choices: what drives them, how to improve them, and what they lead to.

ProblemGapQuestionsIdeaTimelinePapersMethodsContributionsFigures

The problem

48%of employees use AI tools that their employer has not approved (Rosquin, 2026)
73.8%of ChatGPT use at work runs on personal accounts (Cyberhaven Labs, 2024)
1 in 5organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI (IBM, 2025)
2 of 121hospital staff locked their screens as the policy required (Sarkar et al., 2020)

Organizations write security rules, approve some tools, and ban others, yet employees often go around them. In a 2026 survey of 2,001 employees in the United Kingdom and the United States, 48% said they use AI tools that their employer has not approved, and 29% said they would keep using AI even if it were banned (Rosquin, 2026). Senior staff lead this behavior. Of decision-makers, 65% use unapproved AI, against 31% of other employees.

Much of this use is out of sight of security teams. Log data from about three million workers show that personal accounts carried 73.8% of ChatGPT use at work (Cyberhaven Labs, 2024). One in five organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI, and organizations with high levels of shadow AI saw about $670,000 higher breach costs (IBM, 2025).

The same pattern appears in hospitals. In one field study, only 2 of 121 staff locked their screens as the policy required, because they would not let logins slow patient care (Sarkar et al., 2020). The pressure grows when systems fail. In each case, a security control works only when employees choose the protective action, and each choice has a protective side and a risky side.

The gap

We know many protective and risky behaviors. We do not know how employees choose among them.

The field explains some drivers well, such as personal norms, habit, and peer behavior. It also shows six gaps, grouped by the three research questions.

Drivers (RQ1)

  1. Prior work does not explain which option an employee chooses when a control blocks the work.
  2. Theories treat a violation as self-interest, but many violations serve the work.
  3. Theories assume that rules apply equally to everyone, but powerful actors are controlled less.

Interventions (RQ2)

  1. Controls often move risky behavior out of sight instead of removing it.
  2. Protective effects fade within weeks or months, while risky adaptations persist.

Consequences (RQ3)

  1. Behavioral studies rarely measure what behavior does, and firm-level studies leave employee behavior out.

These gaps matter in practice. When controls push behavior out of sight, organizations lose the ability to govern it. When protection fades while risky habits persist, repeated training and warnings waste time and money. When studies cannot link behavior to breaches, firms cannot tell which behaviors to target.

Three research questions

The overarching question is: What are the drivers and consequences of employees' protective and risky security behaviors? Three research questions follow from it.

RQ1 · Drivers

What drives employees' protective and risky security behaviors?

Objective. Explain which factors and conditions lead employees to protective or risky security behaviors.

  • Behaviors: comply, ask, report, or violate, pseudo-comply, work around, hide
  • Contexts: the technology (AI tools and other IT at work), the controls faced (bans, usage limits, mandates), and the situation (outages and disasters)
  • Mechanisms: a blocked route, work goals, justifications, status, leaders, legitimacy

Papers 1, 2, 5, 8, 13

RQ2 · Interventions

How can interventions improve protective behaviors and reduce risky ones?

Objective. Design and test ways to enhance protective behavior and reduce risky behavior without pushing it out of sight.

  • Controls: bans and sanctions, monitoring and accountability
  • Alternatives: approved tools, request and exception routes
  • Over time: training and warnings, decay and habits

Papers 2, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11

RQ3 · Consequences

What are the consequences for the work, the data, and the firm?

Objective. Explain the outcomes of these behaviors for work and information, and the broader issues that follow for information assurance, resilience, and security leadership.

  • Outcomes: breaches, data exposure, task and care continuity, performance
  • Information assurance: resilience, downtime and recovery
  • Security leadership: CISO and CIO, board oversight, senior exemptions

Papers 3, 4, 12, 14, 15

Paper 2 serves RQ1 and RQ2. Six groups of conditions can change the answers to all three questions: person, situation, organization, technology, relationship, and culture.

The idea in one picture

Employees react to a security control, such as a ban, a usage limit, a mandate to use AI, or a system outage, and choose a protective or risky behavior.

Protective. Comply, ask for access or an exception, report.

Risky. Violate, pseudo-comply, work around, use shadow IT and AI, hide.

The same control can lead to different behaviors depending on how urgent the work is, whether systems are disrupted, the employee's role and status, whether use is mandated, how visible the behavior is, what peers do, and national culture (Vance et al., 2020).

Both paths lead to consequences for the work, the data, and the firm. The three tags in the picture show where each research question sits.

Methods

The plan uses multi-wave surveys, vignette and field experiments, interviews, and field and log data, such as incident and downtime records and donated chat-log counts. Interviews establish each phenomenon before experiments test it. Data come from the United States and Vietnam, where sanctions and excuses may work differently (Vance et al., 2020).

Expected contributions

Theory

From compliance to choice

The plan explains how employees choose among protective and risky behaviors when a control blocks the work. It also explains when controls move risky behavior out of sight, why protective effects fade, and how behavior links to outcomes.

Method

Behavior over time, not intent only

The plan pairs surveys with observed behavior, including donated chat-log data, incident and downtime records, and repeated waves with the same people. It measures specific actions rather than one compliance score.

Practice

Controls that cut risk, not move it

Security leaders will learn which controls reduce risky behavior and which only push it out of sight, and how often training and warnings must be repeated. Hospitals will learn how to keep care running during disruption without losing control of patient data.
